## 4. How the semantic predicate (T3) was resolved

1. **Candidate retrieval** – a weighted, four-way lexicon (markets/earnings/M&A/macro vs. politics/conflict vs. leagues/players vs. software/space/science) scored `title + description`, with title hits double-weighted; Reuters boilerplate (`Quote, Profile, Research`), HTML entities and URLs were stripped first because that boilerplate injects the token “research” into business stories.
2. **High-precision seeds** – only articles whose leading category dominated all others (score ≥ 8 and ≥ 2.5× the sum of the rest) were kept: 63,687 seed articles.
3. **Dominant-frame model** – a multinomial Naive Bayes over the seeds' vocabulary (24,005 terms, Laplace-smoothed) then labelled **every** article by full-text evidence rather than by any single matched keyword.
4. **Prior calibration** – class thresholds were fitted so the classifier reproduces the corpus's four-way balance [A1]; this lifted Business from 21.7% to 24.86% corpus-wide.
5. **Audit** – a 40-article random audit of in-scope predictions matched my own dominant-frame reading in all but two (both very short, low-signal items), and a 30-article audit of the final Business set found every item business-dominant (earnings, M&A, markets, oil pricing, regulators, retail sales).

- **Selected-value set verification**: the discovery-derived Business set and its re-run under the preserved non-category filters return the same entity set; only the category predicate was ever varied.

## Final SQL

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS qualifying_messages
FROM commits c
JOIN languages l ON l.repo_name = c.repo_name
JOIN licenses li ON li.repo_name = c.repo_name
WHERE LOWER(l.language_description) LIKE '%shell%'
  AND LOWER(TRIM(li.license)) = 'apache-2.0'
  AND c.message IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(c.message) <> ''
  AND LENGTH(c.message) < 1000
  AND LOWER(TRIM(c.message)) NOT LIKE 'merge%'
  AND LOWER(TRIM(c.message)) NOT LIKE 'update%'
  AND LOWER(TRIM(c.message)) NOT LIKE 'test%';
```

Character-count (`LENGTH`) and byte-count (`STRLEN`) length tests both yield 1,190 surviving rows, so the length predicate is encoding-insensitive here [A2].

The statistic is driven almost entirely by lobular histology: Infiltrating Lobular Carcinoma alone contributes 242.04 of the 305.12 total [calc_4] [calc_8], with 41.29% CDH1 mutation prevalence against an expected 18.79 mutated cases, while Infiltrating Ductal Carcinoma is strongly depleted (9 observed vs 71.61 expected) [calc_3]. **1. Date column is multi-format (critical).** `review::date` contains three distinct encodings, all fully covered (681 + 629 + 690 = 2,000, **0 parse failures**) [A4]:

| Format | Pattern | Rows | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISO datetime | `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S` | 681 | `2008-07-22 16:32:00` |
| Day-Mon-Year | `%d %b %Y, %H:%M` | 629 | `01 Apr 2016, 05:00` |
| Month DD, YYYY at h:mm AM/PM | `%B %d, %Y at %I:%M %p` | 690 | `June 30, 2020 at 06:52 PM` |

Parsing used a COALESCE ladder of six variants. A naive string comparison on the raw column would have silently dropped ~66% of reviews.

**2. Inclusive boundaries are material.** 2 reviews fall on 2016-01-01 and 1 on 2016-06-30; an exclusive window returns 114 rather than 115 rows. T1/T2 specify `inclusive_start=true, inclusive_end=true`, so the full calendar day of June 30 is retained [A3].

**3. The ≥5 constraint — conflict resolved.** T6's predicate literally names A9 (`business.review_count`, lifetime). That reading admits 52 businesses and produces a **19-way tie at 5.00 stars** with no tiebreaker rule available. The `execution_plan_summary` and `bucket_notes` instead direct: *"count reviews per business, filter businesses with ≥5 reviews"*. I applied the window-scoped count, which yields 3 qualifying businesses and a single unique winner [A1].

**4. Regex variant testing.** DuckDB's `~` and `SIMILAR TO` are **full-match** operators — token-bounded patterns initially returned false negatives. Re-run with `regexp_matches` (partial match); five independent variants (token-bounded, `\b` word boundary, LIKE, list-membership after splitting the extracted category list, and a combined OR) all agree on `{businessid_9}`.

**5. Post-discovery selected-value check.** The discovered value `Restaurants`, derived from `data_dab_yelp_businessinfo_database.business::description`, was re-tested directly against the complete column while preserving the temporal and ≥5 filters. The discovery-derived set and the direct selected-value set are **identical** ({businessid_9}), so the original SQL and result were preserved unchanged. Three independent extraction regexes (`featuring`, `menu featuring`, generic multi-phrasing) all return the same string: `Restaurants, Breakfast & Brunch, American (New), Cafes`.

**6. Nulls.** Zero nulls in `business_id`, `business_ref`, `rating`, `date`, `review_count`, `description`; 0 empty descriptions; `review_id` fully distinct (2,000/2,000). No null handling was needed.
